questions.stem: Which statement is the formal definition of T(n) = O(f(n))?
choices: There exist c, n0 > 0 such that T(n) <= c f(n) for all n >= n0
There exist c, n0 > 0 such that T(n) >= c f(n) for all n >= n0
T(n) and f(n) differ by at most a constant for all n
questions.explanation: O is an asymptotic upper bound: a constant multiple of f eventually dominates T. Option 1 is the standard definition; option 2 is Omega; option 3 is little-o.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a tight bound, not merely an upper bound?
questions.explanation: Theta gives matching upper and lower bounds. O is upper only, Omega is lower only, o is strict upper.

questions.stem: What is the running time of the standard divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm?
questions.explanation: Two recursive calls on halves plus a linear combine gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n), which solves to Theta(n log n) by the master theorem.

questions.stem: Kadane's linear-time algorithm uses the recurrence OPT[i] = max(OPT[i-1] + A[i], A[i]). What is OPT[i] semantically?
choices: Maximum subarray sum among all subarrays of A[1..i]
Maximum subarray sum ending exactly at index i
questions.explanation: OPT[i] is the best subarray sum that must end at position i. The global answer is max_i OPT[i].

questions.stem: Which is the correct ordering of growth rates from slowest to fastest?
choices: log n, n, n log n, n^2, 2^n, n!
n, log n, n log n, n^2, n!, 2^n
log n, n log n, n, n^2, n!, 2^n
log n, n, n^2, n log n, 2^n, n!
questions.explanation: Standard ordering: log n < n < n log n < n^2 < 2^n < n! for sufficiently large n.

questions.stem: An algorithm with running time O(nW) on 0/1 Knapsack (W = capacity) is called:
questions.explanation: Input size for W is log W bits, so O(nW) is exponential in input size — pseudo-polynomial. This is why Knapsack is NP-complete despite an O(nW) DP.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about O-notation is FALSE?
choices: If T = O(f) and f = O(g), then T = O(g)
If T = O(n^2) then T = Theta(n^2)
questions.explanation: Big-O is only an upper bound; T = O(n^2) leaves room for T to be linear. Transitivity, sum, and product rules all hold.

questions.stem: Why does Algorithm Design treat polynomial time as the threshold of 'efficient'?
choices: Polynomial-time algorithms always run quickly in practice
Polynomial functions are closed under composition and the class P is machine-independent
questions.explanation: Closure under composition plus robustness across reasonable machine models (Cobham-Edmonds thesis) make P a stable notion of tractability.

questions.stem: What is the running time of the naive O(n^3) maximum subarray algorithm?
questions.explanation: Three nested loops over O(n) range each yield Theta(n^3) work.

questions.stem: Which two pieces of analysis must accompany every algorithm in this unit?
choices: Worst-case time bound and average-case time bound
Proof of correctness and worst-case resource bound
Big-O bound and big-Omega bound on space
questions.explanation: The unit is explicit: every algorithm is judged on correctness (proof) plus worst-case time (resource bound).

questions.stem: Suppose T(n) = 3n^2 + 100 n log n + 5n. Which is the tightest correct statement?
questions.explanation: The 3n^2 term dominates; lower-order terms drop and constants are absorbed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between an 'algorithm' and an 'implementation'?
choices: An algorithm is the mathematical recipe; an implementation is a particular realisation in code on a machine
An implementation always runs faster than the abstract algorithm
questions.explanation: The abstraction barrier matters: correctness and complexity are stated about the algorithm; implementations vary by language, compiler and hardware.

questions.stem: How many bits are required to encode an integer in the range [1, W]?
questions.explanation: Binary encoding of a value W uses ceil(log2 W) + 1 bits, i.e. O(log W). This is the key input-size measure for pseudo-polynomial analyses.

questions.stem: Which recurrence describes the divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm?
questions.explanation: Two recursive halves plus a linear combine (best left-suffix + right-prefix) give T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), solving to O(n log n).

questions.stem: If T(n) = O(n) and S(n) = O(n^2), what is the best bound on T(n) + S(n)?
questions.explanation: Sum rule: O(f) + O(g) = O(max(f, g)) = O(n^2).

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a property of Big-Theta?
questions.explanation: Big-Theta is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive. It is not antisymmetric (many distinct functions are mutually Theta-equivalent).

questions.stem: What does it mean to say 'algorithm A is asymptotically faster than B'?
choices: A's running time is smaller than B's on every input
A's running time grows slower than B's as n -> infinity (eventually)
A uses fewer instructions per iteration
A is implemented in a faster programming language
questions.explanation: Asymptotic comparison is about growth rate for large n, ignoring constants and small-n behaviour.

questions.stem: Which is the correct minimum pass mark on the supervised final exam in COMP3027?
questions.explanation: School policy: at least 40% on the final exam is required to pass, regardless of total mark.

questions.stem: For the cubic max-subarray algorithm, the innermost loop is recomputing what?
choices: The sum A[i] + ... + A[j] from scratch
questions.explanation: Each iteration restarts the inner sum, doing O(n) work that the quadratic version absorbs by maintaining a running total.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about T(n) = n log n?
questions.explanation: n log n grows faster than n but slower than any n^{1+epsilon}, so it is O(n^2) but not O(n) or Omega(n^2).

questions.stem: Which problem framing pattern best fits 'three abstractions' from Lecture 1?
questions.explanation: Lecture 1 names the three abstractions as problem (input/output spec), algorithm (recipe), and analysis (proof + bound).

questions.stem: Which best characterises when log-factor differences matter in practice?
choices: When n is very large, e.g. n = 10^6 or more, factor of ~20 can be the difference between minutes and seconds
questions.explanation: At n = 10^6 a log-factor is ~20x; combined with constants this swings real running time considerably.

questions.stem: If an algorithm's runtime is T(n) = 2^{log n} * n, what is its asymptotic class?
questions.explanation: 2^{log n} = n, so T(n) = n * n = Theta(n^2).

questions.stem: Which is NOT a standard step in stating a problem precisely?
choices: Specify the input type and constraints
Specify the desired output and what counts as correct
questions.explanation: A problem is a mathematical specification of inputs and outputs; code is part of an implementation, not the problem definition.

questions.stem: Why is worst-case (rather than average-case) the default analysis lens in this unit?
choices: Worst case is easier to compute
It gives guarantees that hold for every input, including adversarial ones
Worst case equals average case for most algorithms
questions.explanation: Worst-case bounds are robust: a worst-case bound holds for any input distribution, including adversarial workloads.
